strengths: Timely and practically valuable research direction: extending critic-free group-based policy optimization (e.g., GRPO/DAPO) to LLM-based multi-agent systems, significantly mitigating the memory footprint and training instability of traditional MAPPO.

Well-motivated rollout sampling schemes: the paper systematically formulates and compares homogeneous sampling (IS) and heterogeneous group sampling (FoF and Round-Robin), providing clear trade-offs between computational overhead and agent co-adaptation.

Solid empirical performance and efficiency gains: on multi-hop QA benchmarks (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue), MHGPO variants outperform both zero-shot/unoptimized baselines and MAPPO while substantially reducing GPU memory and per-step wall-clock time.

Insightful qualitative and behavioral analysis: the analysis of training stability, format compliance, output token/query length dynamics, and the progression of intra-group similarity provides good intuition into why heterogeneous group optimization stabilizes over training.
weaknesses: Limited evaluation topology: although presented as a general framework for multi-agent systems, the empirical evaluation is strictly restricted to a single, fixed sequential pipeline (Rewriter -> Reranker -> Answerer). The applicability and scaling of MHGPO to complex topologies (e.g., cyclic agent discussions, hierarchical routing, or dynamic multi-turn interactions) remain unverified.

Heuristic credit assignment: backward reward propagation uses simple averaging across downstream successors (Equation 4) without deeper agent-level credit assignment (such as counterfactual baselines, difference rewards, or value-based attribution). While simple, this may suffer from credit misattribution in longer agent chains.

Theoretical justification of heterogeneous group normalization: computing relative advantages across heterogeneous inputs violates the typical assumption of GRPO (where samples are i.i.d. rollouts from the identical prompt). While Section 4 ('Question 4') offers intuitive explanations, formal analysis of advantage variance and gradient bias is absent.

Baseline scope: comparisons are primarily made against MAPPO and non-RL settings; comparing against or discussing other non-critic alignment baselines adapted to agents (e.g., multi-agent DPO or iterative rejection sampling) would strengthen the empirical claims.

strengths: Timely and practically motivated adaptation of critic-free group relative policy optimization (GRPO) to multi-agent LLM systems, addressing the substantial memory overhead and training instability of MAPPO.
Well-designed multi-agent rollout sampling strategies (FoF and RR) that balance exploration, training efficiency, and inter-agent dependency modeling under parameter sharing.

Clear empirical improvements over MAPPO across multiple multi-hop question answering benchmarks (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, and MuSiQue), demonstrating both in-domain gains and out-of-domain transferability.
Substantial resource efficiency gains, showing notable reductions in GPU memory footprint (~51-58% vs ~82%) and step execution time compared to MAPPO.
Informative behavioral analyses, including tracking the progression of agent-level output patterns, intra-group similarity collapse over training, and agent-specific constraint penalties.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is restricted to a single, linear 3-agent pipeline (Rewriter -> Reranker -> Answerer). The framework is claimed to generalize to general multi-agent systems, but no non-linear, cyclic, or branching collaborative topologies are evaluated.

Lack of direct comparison with a unified single-agent RL baseline (e.g., standard GRPO applied to a single agent invoking search tools via ReAct/interleaved reasoning), which makes it difficult to assess how much benefit comes strictly from the multi-agent decomposition versus end-to-end RL itself.

Heuristic nature of heterogeneous group advantage estimation: in GRPO, baseline subtraction assumes samples share the same prompt. Normalizing rewards across heterogeneous inputs (arising from different previous agent rollouts) introduces confounding state-dependent reward variances that are not theoretically analyzed.

Evaluation is limited to a single LLM family and scale (Llama-3.1-Instruct-8B) and exclusively on multi-hop QA tasks, leaving open whether the observations hold across larger base models or diverse multi-agent domains (e.g., code collaboration or multi-tool planning).

strengths: Timely and practical motivation: Adapting group-based policy optimization (GRPO) to multi-agent LLM systems addresses a major bottleneck in LLM-MARL by removing the memory-heavy and unstable critic networks required by MAPPO.

Well-designed rollout sampling strategies: The paper systematically explores three group rollout strategies (Independent Sampling, Fork-on-first, and Round-robin) to navigate the trade-offs between inter-agent dependency modeling and computational efficiency.

Solid empirical efficiency gains: Demonstrates clear computational and memory advantages over MAPPO (reducing GPU memory usage from ~82% to ~51-57% and lowering step training time) while achieving competitive or superior QA performance across HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, and MuSiQue.

Insightful behavioral and diagnostic analysis: Provides meaningful qualitative and quantitative diagnostics, including training stability curves, format compliance penalties, agent output length/count evolution, and an analysis of how heterogeneous prompt diversity diminishes over training.
weaknesses: Limited agent topologies: The method is motivated as general multi-agent reinforcement learning for LLMs, but experimental verification is restricted to a strictly linear, sequential 3-agent search pipeline (Rewriter -> Reranker -> Answerer). Evaluating on more complex interaction structures (e.g., multi-agent debate, cyclic routing, or dynamic branching) would significantly substantiate generality.

Theoretical concerns regarding heterogeneous baseline estimation: Computing relative reward advantages across different inputs (heterogeneous groups in FoF and RR) introduces potential estimation bias when individual inputs vary substantially in difficulty. While the empirical transition toward homogeneous inputs is observed, a formal analysis or ablation on how this input heterogeneity affects gradient variance/bias is lacking.

Evaluation on a single model family and size: Experiments are only conducted using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Evaluating across multiple model families (e.g., Qwen-2.5) or diverse parameter scales would strengthen empirical confidence.

Lack of statistical significance reporting: Results are reported for a single training run without multiple random seeds, error bars, or significance tests, which is especially important for RL training trajectories.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely challenge in multi-agent LLM systems: replacing compute-heavy, unstable critic networks in MARL (such as MAPPO) with an efficient, critic-free group-relative policy optimization framework.

Well-motivated algorithm design: the combination of backward reward propagation and heterogeneous group rollout strategies (FoF, RR) specifically targets cross-trajectory credit assignment across disjoint agent contexts.

Thorough empirical evaluation: MHGPO demonstrates clear gains in QA performance (Accuracy, EM, F1) on HotpotQA and out-of-domain benchmarks (2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue) while significantly reducing GPU memory footprint and wall-clock training step latency compared to MAPPO.

Comprehensive ablations and analyses, including training dynamics, agent-specific reward penalties vs. task rewards, role-wise freezing experiments, and an insightful theoretical equivalence link to single-transcript GRPO in Appendix D.
weaknesses: The experimental scope is restricted to a single fixed sequential three-agent pipeline (Rewriter -> Reranker -> Answerer) on multi-hop QA tasks; the framework is not empirically tested on non-linear, dynamic, or looping multi-agent topologies.
Experiments are conducted using only one base LLM architecture (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), leaving the generalizability across different model families and scales unverified.

The regrouping mechanism in the Round-robin (RR) strategy partitions unrelated singletons across a batch into comparison groups, which introduces cross-prompt variance into the advantage normalization that lacks rigorous theoretical grounding.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated approach: Extending critic-free group-based policy optimization (GRPO) to multi-agent systems avoids the prohibitive memory footprint and training instability associated with multi-agent critic networks (e.g., MAPPO).

Thorough exploration of rollout sampling strategies: The comparison between Independent Sampling (IS), Fork-on-First (FoF), Round-Robin (RR), and FoF with over-sampling provides clear practical insights into the efficiency–effectiveness trade-offs in multi-agent group rollouts.

Strong and consistent empirical performance: MHGPO consistently outperforms unoptimized MAS, MAPPO, and single-agent RAG/RL baselines (such as Search-o1 and R1-Searcher) across both in-domain (HotpotQA) and out-of-domain (2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue) benchmarks, while demonstrating significant savings in GPU memory and training time.

Comprehensive analysis and ablations: The paper provides extensive ablations on role freezing, backward reward aggregation functions, format penalties, group size sensitivity, and insightful empirical analysis on progressive group homogenization.

Clear theoretical grounding: The authors establish a formal connection between MHGPO and single-context GRPO under context-sufficiency assumptions, clarifying the theoretical continuum between single-transcript reasoning traces and modular multi-agent pipelines.
weaknesses: Restricted experimental topology: Evaluation is limited to a single, fixed three-agent linear pipeline (Rewriter -> Reranker -> Answerer) on multi-hop QA benchmarks. It remains unverified how well the method generalizes to non-linear, branching, or dynamic multi-turn agent interaction topologies.

Limited model scale diversity: Experiments are conducted exclusively with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as the shared backbone. Evaluating across different model families or varying parameter scales would strengthen the understanding of how policy capacity influences heterogeneous advantage estimation.

Heuristic nature of advantage estimation under partial observability: The theoretical equivalence to GRPO rests on context sufficiency (Assumption A3), which practical modular systems typically violate. While empirical results confirm stability, a rigorous theoretical analysis of the gradient variance introduced by heterogeneous grouping under incomplete local contexts remains open.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated adaptation of critic-free group-based policy optimization (e.g., GRPO) to multi-agent systems, replacing compute- and memory-heavy centralized critics (MAPPO) with heterogeneous group relative advantage estimation.

Solid theoretical anchor in Section 4.3 and Appendix D establishing when MHGPO reduces to single-transcript GRPO under parameter sharing and context sufficiency, which helps clarify the theoretical assumptions behind heterogeneous grouping.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation comparing against standard standalone LLMs, unoptimized MAS, single-context search-reasoning baselines (Search-o1, R1-Searcher), and MAPPO, showing consistent improvements across in-domain (HotpotQA) and out-of-domain (2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue) multi-hop QA benchmarks.

Detailed analysis of computational efficiency (GPU memory and step time), training dynamics, group sampling variants (IS, FoF, RR, FoF(os)), reward aggregation operators, and individual agent output stability.
weaknesses: Evaluations are restricted to a single fixed, linear 3-agent topology (Rewriter -> Reranker -> Answerer) on extractive/multi-hop QA. The generality of MHGPO to dynamic, branching, or cyclical agent topologies remains unvalidated.

The framework relies heavily on parameter sharing (a single LLM acting as all agents). While standard in recent LLM-MARL setups, this prevents using heterogeneous specialist models of varying sizes or architectures.

Credit assignment via backward propagation relies on simple averaging, which can be noisy when downstream failures are caused by factors outside an upstream agent's control, though heterogeneous cross-trajectory advantage estimation partially mitigates this.
